title: A cop's case for Flock  - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: A serving US police officer (formerly of the London Met) argues that Flock Safety's automatic license plate recognition cameras measurably raise crime-clearance rates and, contrary to the sudden 2026 political backlash that has seen 150+ cities cancel contracts, make policing more surgical and less invasive rather than more.

themes.theme: How Flock's ALPR technology actually works

insights.claim: Flock Safety is an Atlanta-based startup founded in 2017 that sells small solar-powered automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) cameras mounted on roadside poles, which photograph passing vehicles, log identifying features like color and make, read the plate, and instantly check it against the FBI's national database of stolen cars or wanted persons, alerting nearby officers on a match.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Describes the core product mechanics underpinning Flock's ~$550M+ police-tech business model and why it scaled faster than legacy ALPR installations.
insights.quote: As a car passes, the device takes a photograph of the vehicle, notes identifying features like color and make, and reads its license plate.

insights.claim: Flock's cameras cannot search for or identify individuals and cannot show who is driving a scanned vehicle; even when an alert flags a vehicle linked to a wanted felon, an officer must independently establish who is behind the wheel before there is probable cause to stop it.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the most damaging misuse allegation (facial/person tracking) and is central to Flock's legal defensibility.
insights.quote: What Flock cannot do is search for individuals or show who is driving a particular vehicle that it scans.

insights.claim: Officers using Flock can run 'lookup' searches filtered by partial vehicle descriptions (e.g., a white Toyota Tacoma with a roof rack) within a specific timeframe and area, and can build their own shareable 'hotlists' of plates for ongoing investigations such as drug supply chains or suspended-license drivers, separate from FBI-maintained lists.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows Flock functions as an investigative intelligence tool, not just a passive alert system, expanding its addressable use cases beyond stolen-vehicle recovery.

insights.claim: ALPR technology is not new: it was originally developed in 1976 by the British Home Office, first deployed as a toll-road and tunnel prototype, and led to the first ALPR-enabled arrest in 1981 when a stolen car being driven by its thief was caught.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Undercuts the framing of ALPR as a novel, untested surveillance technology; it has a 50-year deployment history to draw evidence from.

insights.claim: The UK's 'Project Laser' in 2004 was the first large-scale ALPR trial, with cameras reading over five million British license plates and producing 3,071 arrests; a year later ALPR was used to locate a man who had murdered a female police officer, prompting Chief Superintendent Geoff Dodd of West Yorkshire Police to call it 'the best investigative tool we have had since the introduction of DNA analysis'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Gives an early, large-sample UK precedent investors and policymakers can point to when assessing ALPR's efficacy claims decades before Flock existed.
insights.quote: the best investigative tool we have had since the introduction of DNA analysis

insights.claim: In London, ALPR is so embedded in criminal culture that rapper Central Cee references it in lyrics, warning listeners not to smoke weed in cars because of the cameras ('Bare A[L]PR, bro').
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A cultural signal that ALPR changes real-world criminal behavior (deterrence), which is otherwise invisible in crime statistics.
insights.locator: Criminals have learned to fear the technology

insights.claim: Flock's pricing model of roughly $3,000 per camera per year made ALPR affordable to nearly any US police department, given the typical department's annual budget of about $1 million, driving adoption to nearly 30 percent of US police agencies subscribing to the service.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains Flock's rapid market penetration versus legacy ALPR vendors that required expensive fixed installations only large departments could afford.
insights.locator: Flock's idea was to sell a more accurate ALPR camera

insights.claim: American police currently solve only 8.2 percent of reported vehicle thefts with an arrest, but a working paper found that agencies adopting ALPR devices saw a 15.9 percent relative increase in car thefts cleared by arrest, which would raise the national clearance rate to about 9.5 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Quantifies a measurable, study-backed uplift in clearance rates that Flock and rivals can cite in sales pitches and policy defenses.

insights.claim: In Atlantic City, New Jersey, vehicles were involved in 53 percent of shootings in the two years before the city expanded its ALPR network; after the expansion, the city saw monthly average motor vehicle thefts fall 20 percent, property crimes fall 34 percent, and fatal shootings fall almost 40 percent, with 72 alert-triggered traffic stops recovering 40 stolen vehicles and 9 stolen plates.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: One of the strongest single-city natural experiments cited in the piece; a before/after case study likely to be reused in policy debates and vendor marketing.

insights.claim: Flock Safety's own internal study claims that 10 percent of all reported crime in the United States is now solved using evidence obtained from its cameras.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A vendor-sourced, unverified figure — useful as a headline claim but should be treated skeptically given the source is Flock itself, not an independent study.
insights.quote: 10 percent of all reported crime in the United States is solved using evidence obtained from their cameras

insights.claim: Before ALPR, imprecise vague descriptions forced police to stop every vehicle matching a rough description (e.g., every silver Volkswagen Golf in the area for an entire shift), and even after early ALPR was introduced, human filtering layers delayed alerts by five to ten minutes, by which time the target car was usually long gone.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Illustrates the baseline counterfactual — how much broader and more invasive policing was before precise, near-real-time ALPR alerts existed.
insights.quote: There was no audit trail of our mistakes because there was no software.
insights.locator: I can remember policing without ALPR

insights.claim: In the month before publication, Flock cameras became one of the most reviled pieces of street furniture in America — sawn from poles, smashed by teenagers, and rammed by vehicles — with more than 150 cities and towns deactivating their cameras or canceling contracts, even in cities where audits found no evidence of officer misuse.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A fast-moving, material contract-cancellation wave directly threatens Flock Safety's recurring subscription revenue base and signals political/regulatory risk for the whole ALPR sector.
insights.quote: the most reviled piece of street furniture in America

insights.claim: Opposition to Flock spans an unusual left-right political coalition, from Senator Bernie Sanders to former WWE wrestler Kane, now the Republican mayor of Knox County, Tennessee, who has called Flock 'unconstitutional'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cross-partisan opposition suggests the backlash is not a niche or purely partisan issue but a broad public-trust/moral-panic dynamic, raising durability risk for ALPR contracts nationally.

insights.claim: The author frames the sudden backlash against Flock as joining a recognizable pattern of American moral panics, comparing it to prior public scares over data centers, Covid vaccines, 5G towers, pasteurized milk, and fracking.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A framework for reading the backlash as sentiment-driven and potentially transient rather than evidence-driven, which matters for forecasting whether cancellations stick or reverse.
insights.quote: has joined data centers, Covid vaccines, 5G towers, pasteurized milk and fracking in the pantheon of American moral panics
insights.locator: Over the space of a few weeks

insights.claim: The author argues the political backlash against Flock is structurally driven by an asymmetry of visibility: a crime prevented because an offender feared ALPR produces no victim and no police report, while every instance of misuse produces a visible victim, a mugshot of a corrupt officer, or a photo of an innocent motorist in handcuffs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A generalizable mental model for why effective but invisible-benefit technologies (surveillance, predictive policing, vaccines) face outsized political risk relative to their measured harms.
insights.quote: a crime prevented because an offender was afraid of being caught by ALPR produces no victim and no police report

insights.claim: Every Flock search must be logged with a case number and recorded reason, published in a monthly audit reviewed by department administrators; suspicious searches are flagged by algorithms or department audits and the offending user is blocked from the system until senior officers review and resolve the flag.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Describes the compliance architecture that differentiates Flock from unaudited surveillance tools and that Flock could expand as a policy concession to regulators.
insights.locator: each search in Flock must be accompanied by a recorded reason

insights.claim: Flock has reduced data retention from thirty days to just seven days for recorded plate scans, a recent policy change made in response to privacy concerns.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable concession Flock has already made that could be highlighted in future lobbying or PR to blunt the backlash, and a metric to track if further shortened.
insights.locator: Results were originally retained for thirty days

insights.claim: The Institute for Justice, a think tank critical of ALPR, studied Flock misuse in April of the same year and found 51 documented misuse incidents across the United States since 2024, noting that nearly all of the officers involved were criminally charged and lost their jobs, either by resigning or being fired.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Even a critical watchdog's own count of confirmed abuse (51 cases against ~30% of ~18,000 US police agencies subscribing) is a small base rate, which is central to the author's proportionality argument against blanket bans.
insights.quote: Nearly all of these officers were criminally charged and lost their jobs, either by resigning or getting fired

insights.claim: Documented misuse of Flock has included officers stalking ex-partners using the system, and separately, innocent motorists have been wrongly stopped after cameras misread plates or matched stale/incorrect entries in national databases — a recurring failure mode being stolen front license plates entered into the database leading to innocent owners of the corresponding rear plate being detained on suspicion of car theft.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Names the specific, recurring technical failure mode (front/rear plate mismatch) that Flock or regulators could target with a low-cost fix to reduce false-positive stops.
insights.quote: A common issue from my experience is stolen front license plates being entered into a database
insights.locator: There are stories of police officers

insights.claim: The author concedes Flock does not stop a corrupt officer from simply following a car they dislike the look of, or manually writing down plates seen outside an ex-partner's house — such abuse becomes harder to catch, not impossible, meaning the audit trail only catches misuse that goes through the system itself.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: An honest limitation acknowledgment — the audit trail reduces but does not eliminate the risk surface, which is a nuance regulators and civil-liberties groups will keep pressing on.
insights.quote: there is nothing to stop a corrupt officer simply following a car when they don’t like the look of its driver
insights.locator: While Flock is a tool that can be audited

insights.claim: Contrary to a widespread claim among critics, Flock cameras do not scan or track passing phones or other devices — they only capture vehicle and plate images.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts a specific misinformation vector fueling the backlash, relevant for anyone modeling how much of the public panic rests on factually incorrect claims.
insights.locator: Another incorrect belief is that Flock does more than scan vehicles

insights.claim: US courts have repeatedly held over the last century that police observation of license plates, whether by naked eye or machine, is not an unreasonable search, because a license plate belongs to the government and is displayed in a public place.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Establishes the legal foundation that makes a nationwide ALPR ban constitutionally unlikely, which matters for assessing long-term regulatory risk to Flock and its rivals.
insights.locator: But it has been repeatedly established

insights.claim: In 1983 the US Supreme Court unanimously held that a person traveling in an automobile on public roads has no reasonable expectation of privacy regarding their movements from one place to another; in January 2026 a federal judge in Virginia ruled against two civil rights activists in a challenge specifically targeting Flock, finding that a single license plate scan does not invade any privacy interest.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A very recent (2026) federal court win for Flock specifically, giving the company near-term legal cover even as political and municipal-contract pressure mounts — an important divergence between legal risk (low) and political/reputational risk (high).
insights.quote: An individual scan of a license plate, a vehicle identifier that generally must be displayed under state law, does not invade any privacy interests
insights.locator: in January of 2026, a federal judge in Virginia ruled

themes.theme: Market structure and second-order policy effects

insights.claim: Flock does not have a monopoly on ALPR: at least five other companies offer nearly identical products and services to public and private customers, some arguably more invasive than Flock, and several cities that canceled their Flock contracts have since signed up with Flock's rivals instead.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Suggests the backlash is targeting Flock's brand specifically rather than ALPR as a category, meaning canceled Flock revenue may simply transfer to competitors rather than disappear — a key read for anyone assessing Flock Safety's competitive moat and business risk.
insights.locator: Flock did not invent its capabilities

insights.claim: The author predicts America is unlikely to ban ALPR at either the state or national level; instead a policy patchwork will emerge with practices diverging by local and political jurisdiction, similar to existing fragmentation in American policing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A base-rate forecast investors in Flock or its competitors should weight: expect fragmented, city-by-city regulatory risk rather than a uniform federal ban.
insights.quote: It seems unlikely that America will ever ban ALPR at a state level, let alone a national one.

insights.claim: Even where police departments dismantle their Flock networks, the cameras will not disappear because the Fourth Amendment only restrains government action, not private enterprise — homeowners associations and other private buyers can and already do purchase their own private ALPR camera networks.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Identifies a private-sector demand channel (HOAs, private security) that is structurally immune to municipal contract cancellations, a potential resilient revenue segment for ALPR vendors even amid public-sector backlash.
insights.locator: Police departments may dismantle their networks

insights.claim: The author argues the residents most harmed by police departments canceling Flock contracts will be those in small towns whose departments cannot afford helicopters, drones, or enough officers to patrol every road themselves — i.e., the poorest-resourced jurisdictions lose the most crime-fighting capability.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reframes the backlash as regressive in effect: well-resourced cities have alternatives (drones, helicopters, more officers) that small under-resourced departments lack, meaning contract cancellations disproportionately hurt smaller communities.
insights.quote: The people harmed the most will be the residents of the average small town whose police departments cannot afford helicopters, drones or enough police officers

insights.claim: The author's central contrarian claim is that Flock's critics are right that police should invade law-abiding citizens' lives as little as possible, but wrong about what Flock does — the technology in practice lets officers be more surgical and precise, reducing the number of innocent people pulled over compared to policing without it.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The essay's thesis in a sentence: reframes ALPR as a privacy-protective technology relative to the pre-ALPR baseline of broad, imprecise stops, directly countering the current political narrative driving contract cancellations.
insights.quote: Flock allows us to be more surgical and precise, avoiding pulling over innocent people with all of the risks that involves. More than anything, Flock allows me to leave you alone.
insights.locator: Flock's critics have the important point right

insights.claim: Almost half of US police departments (nearly 50 percent) employ fewer than ten full-time officers, and the country has four million miles of public roads, which the author cites as structural reasons why manual, human-only license-plate tracking was hopelessly outmatched by criminals before ALPR.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Establishes the resource-scarcity baseline that makes low-cost automated tools like Flock disproportionately valuable to small, underfunded departments rather than large urban forces.
insights.quote: America has four million miles of public roads, and almost 50 percent of the country’s police departments employ fewer than ten full-time officers.
